item.title: A Photo of Mussolini’s Corpse Led Page 1. How It Got There Is a Tale.
item.description:
This story is part of a series marking 175 years of eyewitness journalism from The New York Times. Read more here.

It was an incredible thing to see firsthand: the battered bodies of the deposed Italian fascist leader Benito Mussolini and his lover, Clara Petacci, dumped like so much rubbish in a public square in Milan in the waning days of World War II. The New York Times correspondent Milton Bracker was there on that day, April 29, 1945 — nine days before VE day, the end of the war in Europe — to take the measure of the moment.

“Benito Mussolini came back last night to the city where his fascism was born,” Bracker wrote in a front-page article in the next day’s paper. “He came back on the floor of a closed moving van, his dead body flung on the bodies of his mistress and 12 men shot with him.”

Bracker’s account, written in the first person with an unusual undercurrent of moral indignation, reflected the gravity of the event, the sense that history had swerved suddenly in a new direction. It told how, his support crumbling away, Mussolini had driven north in an attempt to escape to Switzerland. Before he got there, Bracker wrote, he was caught, “like the fleeing Marie Antoinette.”

The story was packed with details. Mussolini’s speedy trial and summary execution by a firing squad along with a group of his followers in Giulino di Mezzegra, in northern Italy. How their bodies were heaped in a van and deposited in the Piazzale Loreto in Milan, of symbolic importance “because recently 15 patriots were executed there.”

The bodies were then savagely attacked by angry partisans. Bracker said he and other American reporters had been “thrust into the circle of death” by onlookers eager to show them what had happened.

An unknown photographer shows the reporter at the scene in his military uniform, notebook in hand, interviewing a soldier while the corpses of Mussolini and his mistress lay sprawled at their feet. Bracker saw two young men viciously kicking the slain dictator’s head, causing a “hideous crunch that wholly disfigured the once-proud face,” he wrote.

“It was naturally one of the grimmest moments of our lives, but it will at least serve to give absolutely authentic eyewitness accounts,” he added.

It is one thing to read about such an event in a newspaper; it’s another thing to see a picture of it. Bracker’s story was accompanied by a four-column, front-page photograph depicting the chaotic scene: the bodies of Mussolini and Petacci atop the pile of corpses — Mussolini is easily identifiable by his bald head — as a crowd of armed onlookers pushes and jostles alongside them.

The following day, May 1, the paper printed two additional photographs. One showed the corpses of Mussolini, Petacci and others dangling by their ankles from a pole at an abandoned service station, where they had been strung up by the mob; another showed Lieut. Gen. Achille Starace, an ally of Mussolini, in the final moments before his own execution by a firing squad.

The publication of these photographs was a coup for The Times. Transmitting photos around the world in the age of the internet is such a smooth undertaking that it’s easy to forget how difficult it once was. In the early days of news photography, the only method to get a photo from one place to another was to physically transport the film — an exercise in delayed gratification if, say, it involved a journey by boat across the Atlantic.

A breakthrough came in the 1920s with the development of practical radiophoto technology, a technique by which photographs were scanned and their tones converted into electrical pulses. The pulses were then sent wirelessly to New York, in the case of The Times, where they were transformed back into photographic images for publication.

Along with several other major news organizations, including The Chicago Tribune and The Christian Science Monitor, The Times in 1929 set up a company called Press Wireless that bypassed commercial telegraph monopolies. The company built its own shortwave radio transmission and receiving stations, allowing its members to transmit articles and images far more efficiently.

But transmission was still subject to logistical challenges, particularly during war. At the time of Mussolini’s death, the Press Wireless transmitting office nearest to Milan was in Geneva, some 155 miles away as the crow flies. So in order to get the photographs — which were taken by an Italian photographer whose name remains stubbornly lost to time — to New York, someone first had to get them to Geneva.

Bracker was busy writing his article, the first draft of history. But the mysterious photographer knew Daniel T. Brigham, a Times correspondent based in Bern, Switzerland, and offered to personally transport the photos to Ponte Chiasso, on the Italian-Swiss border, and put them on a train bound for Bern.

Even that was no easy task in a country ravaged by war. The photographer had to hitchhike to the border, navigating “highways blocked with bewildered countrymen and kept in ferment by roving partisan bands,” Meyer Berger, a former Times correspondent, wrote in his book about The Times’s first century, “The Story of The New York Times 1851-1951.” But the photographer got there and put the package on the train.

“Oh, boy, have I got something special!” Brigham exclaimed when he called The Times late that night to say that he had collected the package in Bern. He asked the Press Wireless office, normally closed on Sunday, to prepare to receive his transmission. Meanwhile, he got ready to go to Geneva.

After scrounging up gas for the trip, and obtaining permission from a military censor to use the photos, Brigham set off alone on a dangerous Alpine drive in the middle of the night. “He headed into a mountain blizzard, careening and skidding over black precipices on the dark and narrow alpine roads,” Berger wrote. At one point, one of his tires blew out, and Brigham had to change it in the storm.

At 11:30 p.m. New York time — 5:30 a.m. in Geneva — the images began to emerge from the Press Wireless’s receiver at The Times. They arrived too late for the first edition. But after some changes to the paper’s layout by the night managing editor, Raymond H. McCaw, the first photo, of Mussolini lying in the pile of corpses, was placed on the front page for the second edition.

It was rare to print such a graphic image in the paper, especially on the front page. But the photographs were irrefutable proof that Mussolini was dead. And they were a crucial visual complement to the story of what happened, told in Bracker’s accompanying article and analyzed in a Times editorial that same day.

“The wretched end of Benito Mussolini marks a fitting end to a wretched life,” the editorial said. “The man who once boasted that he was going to restore the glories of ancient Rome is now a corpse in a public square in Milan, with a howling mob cursing and kicking and spitting on his remains.”

After putting the paper to bed, McCaw typed out a memo to the publisher, Arthur Hays Sulzberger, with the time at the top, 1:15 a.m.

“Mr. Sulzberger: I think you will agree that the Mussolini picture was well worth Page 1,” he wrote. “Personally, I think that next to the Iwo Jima flag-raising this was the second-best picture of the year,” he added, referring to the famous photo, by Joe Rosenthal of The Associated Press, of six Marines raising the American flag on the island of Iwo Jima two months earlier.

Sulzberger’s Western Union message to Brigham in Bern later that day was presumably no less heartfelt, despite being written in the weird unpunctuated syntax peculiar to telegrams. “Congratulations securing Mussolini picture which unique,” he wrote.

item.title: U.N. Warns Against Technology Used to Read Citizens’ Minds
item.description:
The scenarios sound like science fiction: Police officers accessing data contained in suspects’ brains to forcefully extract information, or to predict if offenders might plan to commit future crimes.

But the secretary-general of the United Nations warned on Thursday for the first time that neurotechnologies are advancing so rapidly that governments’ ability to access and manipulate people’s brains could one day pose a threat to fundamental human rights.

The abuse of future technologies, Secretary-General António Guterres warned, could lead to arbitrary detentions, the alteration of people’s mental states and infringements on privacy.

“Neurotechnology, including new and emerging forms, raises profound human rights challenges when applied to the administration of justice,” the secretary-general wrote. “Its expansion beyond clinical settings into investigative, judicial and correctional contexts introduces significant risks, alongside potential benefits.”

To address such threats, the report lists a number of recommendations, including establishing regulations consistent with international law, recognizing thoughts as “highly sensitive personal data” and requiring explicit consent for the use of neurotechnology in criminal justice settings.

Human rights officials said the document was an important step toward raising global awareness of the issue and that it could help countries develop laws to prevent the abuse of such technology.

“This gives states an opportunity to establish clear rules to regulate the use of neurotechnology, based on human rights, before they become routine in investigations, courts and prisons,” said Jeremy Laurence, a spokesman for the U.N. Human Rights Office.

The report, some rights activists said, broadens the traditional understanding of freedom of thought, which has largely focused on freedom of expression, to include keeping one’s innermost ideas private.

“It’s no longer just about the classical ways through which freedom of thought is evoked,” said Marcello Ienca, a professor of ethics and neuroscience at the Technical University of Munich.

The U.N.’s interest comes amid a growing global push to protect brain data. Chile in 2012 enshrined protections for brain activity in its constitution. And several states, including California, Colorado and Montana, have passed laws protecting neural data. Similar measures have been proposed in Argentina, Brazil, Colombia and Mexico.

But while some countries are working to protect citizens’ neural data, others are already attempting to access it.

In India, the police have for two decades used a technology called Brain Electrical Oscillation Signature — or BEOS — to determine whether a suspect may have been involved in a crime.

The scientific basis for this technology, which reads brain waves, is scant. Results from BEOS tests are inadmissible as evidence in Indian courts, but the technology has been applied in hundreds of high-stakes cases, including those of murder, rape and terrorism.

BEOS has not been validated by the international scientific community. And a committee established by the Indian government to review BEOS concluded in 2008 that it was “sub-optimal.”

Not all neurotechnologies are being developed as tools of the state. Many have been brought to the consumer market as wearable health and wellness gadgets that can help users monitor their stress, sleep and focus.

But those too, experts warned, are subject to few regulations.

The Neurorights Foundation analyzed the privacy policies of 30 consumer neurotechnology companies in 2024 and found that most did not have limits on how they used customers’ brain data. More than half of those companies, the foundation said, explicitly allowed user data to be shared with third parties.

Neurotechnologies have also become powerful clinical tools for patients who have suffered severe brain or spinal cord injuries. Brain-computer interfaces have helped paralyzed patients to write sentences by imagining handwriting, as well as to move robotic limbs and to play chess online just by thinking.

item.title: The Man City Scandal Is About More Than Football
item.description:
Manchester City first came to my attention after we moved from Berlin to Cardiff and my then-8-year-old son, an avid football fan, declared that Man City was now his team. It was 2024, and the club had just won its fourth consecutive Premier League title — unheard of. That was clearly enough for my Welsh son to set aside any misgivings he might have had about supporting an English club.

Those titles don’t look so shiny now. Last month, an independent commission found Man City had broken more than 100 of the league’s financial rules. It said the team, whose majority owner is Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the vice president of the United Arab Emirates, spent hundreds of millions of pounds it wasn’t allowed to spend, on players it could never have otherwise afforded. (Man City is appealing the ruling.)

I spoke to my colleague Tariq Panja, our global sports correspondent, about the biggest financial scandal in football history.

So Tariq, let’s talk about the scandal at Man City. Full disclosure: My 10-year-old is a Man City fan.

He’s not the only one! Kids love a winning team, and this generation of kids only know Man City as a winning team. But historically this was Manchester’s second team. It really wasn’t known for any great success — until Sept. 1, 2008. That’s the day Sheikh Mansour bought the club.

Why did Sheikh Mansour want to own Man City — or any football club for that matter?

Well, it is in the Premier League, which is the biggest league in the world. Millions of people watch it every year. It’s Britain’s biggest soft power export, bar none. For people wanting to burnish their personal image or their country’s image, it’s the epitome of sporting greatness. It gives you immediate name recognition. It’s a shortcut to respectability.

But it also brings scrutiny. Because if he didn’t own Man City, few in Britain would know who Sheikh Mansour is.

And of course that scrutiny has now come back to bite him. So tell me, someone who doesn’t watch the Premier League, what happened?

It’s massive. It’s the biggest financial cheating scandal in the history of football. To put it simply, they cooked the books in order to spend money they weren’t allowed to spend on an array of world-class talent.

You can only spend what you earn. There are three buckets of income for football teams: TV rights, stadium tickets and sponsorship. The first two, you can’t really manipulate. The third one is, according to a panel of arbitrators, the one that they really went to town on.

How so?

They signed a bunch of sham contracts with sponsors — U.A.E.-owned companies, like Etihad Airways. But those companies paid for a tiny fraction of that sponsorship. The rest of it came from Sheikh Mansour’s company, which was padding those numbers to an enormous degree. Of the roughly 950 million pounds of supposed sponsorship money Man City was claiming, only 120 million or so actually came from sponsors.

And all that money allowed it to buy players it would otherwise not have been able to afford?

Exactly. It allowed City to buy one of the best managers, Pep Guardiola, and some of the best players — Kevin De Bruyne, David Silva, Sergio Aguero — and pay them some of the biggest wages in the business. They’ve won eight Premier League titles under Sheikh Mansour’s ownership.

So who was hurt by this?

Where to start? Man City took the best players from so many rival teams over the years. From its traditional rival, Manchester United, from Arsenal, but also from mid-ranking teams like Aston Villa, who for three summers during this period had their best player taken by Man City. It changed the trajectory of lives, of careers, of teams for a decade.

And then there is the financial damage. A place in the Champions League is worth tens of millions of euros a year. So the team that didn’t make the Champions League — because Man City took a spot that should have gone to them — potentially lost huge amounts of revenue, sponsorship and the like.

OK, let’s talk about the politics of this. Is there any potential political cost for Britain in punishing a major Gulf investor?

The politics of this are very tricky. The U.A.E., which is a British ally, now stands accused of corrupting Britain’s biggest cultural export to the world. Bloomberg reported that Emirati officials have warned that a harsh punishment could have consequences for future investments in Britain.

And it’s created a headache for the prime minister, Andy Burnham. Remember, he was mayor of Greater Manchester until recently. He knows these people very well. The huge amount of investment his city attracted over the last decade? Some of that can be linked to Abu Dhabi. So now there is also scrutiny on Burnham and what kind of relationship he had with them.

How do Man City fans feel about all this?

Well, for the past decade, they just rallied around their club. Because this is a core part of their identity. They’re suddenly successful as a club, and here the world is telling them, “You’re cheating.”

But I would say that since the verdict, there has been a change in tone. There are still the zealots who refuse to think it’s anything but a conspiracy. But some are now saying, “Guys, we might have been wrong.” Some are really sad that it’s happened. Some are angry their club was used for this.

What will happen to Man City now?

Everything is on the table because we haven’t seen a scandal like this in the history of the Premier League. It could be relegated — demoted down a division or two. It could be banned from buying talent. Or given a massive penalty on points. Or charged a financial penalty. But some people are calling for it to be thrown out of the league altogether. That would be the most extreme punishment.

Less than a year ago, while her family was spending the holidays in Lagos, Adichie’s 21-month-old son, Nkanu, died. Finally, the Welsh Music Inspiration Award went to Mary Hopkin, an absolute legend. Paul McCartney produced her. She sang backing vocals for David Bowie. Her most famous song is both a masterpiece and a great way to finish the week: “Those Were the Days.”

item.title: How the Epstein Files forced the Nobel Peace Prize to reckon with impartiality.
item.description:
The Nobel Peace Prize is no stranger to scrutiny, with the choice of laureate sometimes inviting hard questions.

This year, the Norwegian committee that awards the prize came under scrutiny itself after a tranche of emails revealed ties between the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and Thorbjorn Jagland, a former head of the committee.

The messages raised concerns about the impartiality of the group’s members — often former Norwegian diplomats and officials — and led to the adoption, for the first time in 125 years, of ethics rules.

The Norwegian Nobel Committee consists of five members chosen by the Norwegian Parliament for a term of six years. Sitting lawmakers are not eligible, and nominees are often drawn from politics and diplomacy. Deliberations for the prize are shrouded in secrecy and, “in the past, verbal clarifications and mutual trust carried a great deal of weight,” the committee said this year.

After the revelations of the ties between Mr. Jagland and Mr. Epstein, who died in prison in 2019, the committee acknowledged change was needed.

“It is no longer enough to point to tradition, history and good intentions,” Jorgen Watne Frydnes, current chairman of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, said when announcing the rules in March.

Committee members are now required to declare their professional affiliations to an internal audit, and they are prohibited from accepting gifts or travel that could be deemed as trying to curry favor.

Haakon Gjerlow, acting director of the Peace Research Institute in Oslo, said that ethical scandals “would erode the dignity of the prize if there were to be a lot of turmoil around the committee year after year.”

Norway has long taken pride in being the country that hands out the prestigious award. But that position has also made the committee’s members a target for lobbying. The committee’s internal deliberations remain confidential for 50 years, and even if a peace prize candidate approaches a committee member, that can only be reported internally.

The emails published this year showed that part of Mr. Epstein’s interest in Norwegian diplomats stemmed from their connection to the Nobel Prize, particularly Mr. Jagland, who is also a former prime minister of Norway. Mr. Jagland is now under investigation by the Norwegian police’s economic crimes unit.

Other prominent Norwegians have faced scrutiny for their ties to Mr. Epstein, including the current queen, Mette-Marit; Borge Brende, a former foreign minister; and Mona Juul, a diplomat.

Some Norwegian politicians believe the Nobel committee needs a wider overhaul. In 2024, the vice chair of the committee, Asle Toje, traveled to Ethiopia as part of a paid consultancy for an Ethiopian mining company, according to a report this year by Aftenposten, a Norwegian newspaper. The trip, disclosed under the committee’s new ethical rules, raised questions over Mr. Toje’s relationship with Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed of Ethiopia, who started a war soon after winning the Nobel Peace Prize in 2019.

Opposition lawmakers in the Green Party of Norway have called for selection criteria that would give more weight to professional expertise and would guard against political affiliation, but the Norwegian Parliament voted against the proposal in June.

Last week, Parliament began a public inquiry into how much influence Mr. Epstein had wielded with Norwegian political elites. Separately, an independent commission of inquiry was also looking into how Norway’s foreign service may have been affected by links to Mr. Epstein.

item.title: Navi Pillay, a South African Human Rights Lawyer, Is Awarded the Nobel Peace Prize
item.description:
Navi Pillay, who won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday, is a South African human rights lawyer who fought against the apartheid regime and who was formerly the United Nations’ top human rights official.

She was recognized “for her efforts to promote peace and international law,” the Norwegian Nobel Committee said in announcing the prize in Oslo.

Last year, a United Nations commission led by Ms. Pillay that was investigating the war in Gaza found that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians, its most sweeping finding yet about the Israeli government’s conduct in the conflict. The Israeli government denounced the report.

The Nobel committee’s statement announcing Ms. Pillay as the winner included only a brief mention of her work on that investigation. Asked about it after the announcement, Jorgen Watne Frydnes, the committee’s chair, said her work on the commission was “an important part of the reasoning why she received the prize.”

The U.N. human rights office welcomed the news.

“Particularly at this time, when human rights are under attack by so many, including so many in powerful positions, this award to Navi Pillay is a testament to how important and how relevant human rights are to everything we do,” said Ravina Shamdasani, spokeswoman for the U.N. human rights chief, Volker Turk.

“Navi Pillay remains an inspiration to millions globally, including her colleagues at the U.N. human rights office.”

item.title: ‘Please Pick Up’: When Nobel Committee Calls, Not Everyone Is Ready to Answer
item.description:
The chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, Jorgen Watne Frydnes, told the world on Friday morning that Navi Pillay had won the Nobel Peace Prize. One person who hadn’t been informed yet: Ms. Pillay.

“My message to her would be: If you see a Norwegian number calling, please pick up,” Mr. Frydnes said at the announcement in Oslo. “I would love to talk to you very soon.”

Ms. Pillay, a South African jurist, was at an annual conference of human rights lawyers and judges in Nuremberg, Germany. When the news of her award broke, Stephen Rapp, a former U.S. ambassador for war crimes issues, said that he “shouted out the news in a room with about 120 people and all broke into applause.”

Ms. Pillay wasn’t the first Nobel laureate that the prize committees in Norway and Sweden have had trouble reaching immediately to share the news. Many weren’t even awake at the time.

It was around 1 a.m. in a “cheap hotel room in California” in 2024 when Geoffrey Hinton, a pioneer of research in artificial intelligence, got a call saying he was a winner of a Nobel Prize in Physics.

He did not know his work was even being considered for the honor. Was it a prank? Or could it be a dream?

“It is a million times more likely to be a dream than a reality,” Dr. Hinton thought.

Either way, one thing was certain: There was a Swedish-accented voice with life-changing news on the other end of the phone.

“It was quite confusing,” Dr. Hinton said.

The surprise is by design. The winners of the Nobel Prizes remain a secret, even to the winners themselves, until hours or minutes before they are publicly announced.

“There’s no heads-up,” said Thomas Perlmann, the secretary-general of the Nobel Assembly, who makes what is always “an interesting phone call” to the winner of the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Each of the six Nobel Prizes is managed by one of four institutions, which all enlist different callers. The only call that originates outside Sweden is the one made to the Nobel Peace Prize winner, who is selected by a five-person committee appointed by the Norwegian Parliament.

The unexpected calls are a last bit of secrecy to protect the process from outside influence, Dr. Perlmann said. But he acknowledged that it added to the “mystique” of it all.

“These calls from Stockholm are quite famous,” Dr. Perlmann said.

Yet those calls sometimes go unanswered.

Paul Milgrom, a professor at Stanford University who was awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 2021, had turned off his cellphone that night, as he does every night. So he found out when Robert B. Wilson, another Stanford economist and his neighbor, rang the doorbell at 2:15 a.m. The two men shared the prize.

“Paul? It’s Bob Wilson. You’ve won the Nobel Prize,” Mr. Wilson said in the moment, which was captured on doorbell camera footage. “And so they’re trying to reach you.”

Mr. Milgrom had long brought Mr. Wilson oranges, apples and figs from his yard, but the news Mr. Wilson brought was even sweeter.

“I was glad to share the moment with him,” Mr. Milgrom said.

Not everyone is happy to be notified in the middle of the night. Dr. Perlmann can think of at least one “incredibly angry” winner roused by his call.

“He became very friendly very fast,” Dr. Perlmann said. “We like to try to reach them before they find out any other way.”

For Dr. Perlmann, the call window is the 90 minutes between when the formal decision and the official announcement are made.

One of last year’s winners in medicine, Fred Ramsdell, was off the grid in the Rocky Mountains and could not be reached before the public announcement. This year’s winners — Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel — were much easier to contact: Mr. Deisseroth is a night owl; the other two were in Germany.

“I got hold of all three,” Dr. Perlmann said. “An easy year, definitely.”

Joel Mokyr won the Nobel in economic science last year but had been blocking calls from unknown numbers for much longer.

“I thought I had a better chance of being elected pope, and I’m Jewish,” Mr. Mokyr said.

item.title: Trump Administration Hits International Criminal Court With Severe Sanctions
item.description:
The Trump administration announced on Friday that it was imposing severe financial sanctions on the International Criminal Court, its latest effort to cripple the global body that seeks to prosecutes war crimes, including genocide, and other serious criminal acts.

The new sanctions, unveiled by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the State Department, would prohibit transactions with the court after a grace period of six months. Any companies doing business with the court afterward could be subject to punishment by the U.S. government. The threat of that could constrain the institution’s ability to carry out daily operations.

Although the State Department had been preparing the sanctions for months, Mr. Rubio’s announcement came just hours after a committee in Norway said it was awarding the Nobel Peace Prize to Navi Pillay, a South African lawyer who served for nine years as a judge on the International Criminal Court and worked as the top human rights official at the United Nations.

The sanctions are an intensification of the Trump administration’s push to undermine the court. In February 2025, just weeks after taking office, President Trump issued an executive order directing agencies to come up with sanctions to impose on the court.

At the time, he said the court was trying to violate American sovereignty and undermine “the critical national security and foreign policy work of the United States government and our allies, including Israel.”

Mr. Rubio said in a statement on Friday that Mr. Trump would never allow the court to prosecute Americans. “We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate,” he said.

Mr. Rubio announced in July that the United States planned to “systematically disable” the court, which Mr. Trump has long described as a threat to Americans.

The administration has imposed financial sanctions and visa bans on court judges and prosectors, but the measures announced on Friday are broader.

item.title: Fine Wines, Brazen Thieves: 30,000 Bottles Stolen in Tuscan Heist
item.description:
A group of men pulled off an astounding wine heist last weekend, stealing 30,000 bottles from a warehouse in Cortona in the Tuscany region of Italy. The wine’s owner estimates that the thieved vino was worth $5.5 million.

While booze is regularly nicked from restaurants and wine shops, Lorenzo Vivoli, who works in communications for Marchesi Antinori, the winemaker that was robbed, said he was not aware of any theft this big directly from a warehouse or winery.

The thieves struck on the evening of Oct. 2. Security video showed that it was a large operation, involving seven or eight masked men who loaded the wine into two trucks, with two more men as drivers. The job took about three hours, Mr. Vivoli said.

While no arrests have been made, there are some suspicions.

The warehouse alarm system did not go off, leading Mr. Vivoli to suspect the involvement of “someone from the inside” who might have deactivated it.

Moreover, the red wines taken were Guado al Tasso, Solaia and Tignanello, some of Marchesi Antinori’s most prestigious and sought-after varieties. Marchesi Antinori is one of Italy’s most venerable wineries, its history dating to the 14th century. It lies in Tuscany, the country’s second-largest wine-exporting region, and perhaps its most famous.

On the Friday evening the wine was stolen, the bottles were sitting in the warehouse, ready to be shipped for export on Monday morning. Those shipments happen only once or twice a year.

“They got the perfect timing,” Mr. Vivoli said. “It’s almost like they knew.”

While the wine bottles have a small label to authenticate them and discourage counterfeiting, the shipment did not have any tracking system built in.

And while the winery had insurance, it was intended to cover smaller-scale thefts. “We weren’t prepared for something like this,” Mr. Vivoli said. “We do have insurance, but unfortunately it will only pay us one-tenth of the price.”

The police in Cortona are investigating. “They are very confident they can go forward in a good way,” Mr. Vivoli said of the police. “30,000 bottles do not disappear.”

Indeed, while the thieves succeeded in their brazen heist, unloading so many bottles may well prove more difficult.

For one thing, the bottles they stole are not random hooch. “These wines are produced in limited quantities that are very sought after,” Mr. Vivoli said. “They are only tiny quantities sent to each restaurant or wine store.”

Marchesi Antinori’s executives hope that its discriminating customers could aid the investigation.

“We are cooperating closely with the authorities and informing our partners and customers around the world, asking them to pay particular attention to any offers outside official distribution channels,” said Renzo Cotarella, the company’s chief executive.

But perhaps the thieves aren’t looking to sell. Could they simply be passionate oenophiles who plan to drink the 30,000 bottles of Tuscan red themselves?

Mr. Vivoli responded with a laugh: “You’d need a lot of thieves.”

item.title: Navi Pillay, South African Jurist, Is Awarded the Nobel Peace Prize
item.description:
A South African lawyer with a long record in human rights work, including leading a U.N. commission that said Israel had committed genocide, won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday, a decision that drew Israel’s condemnation and underscored the country’s deep isolation on the world stage.

The lawyer, Navanethem Pillay, known as Navi, has worked for decades on human rights issues, defending anti-apartheid activists like the future president and Nobel laureate Nelson Mandela. Over the years, she has variously served as a top U.N. official and as a judge on the International Criminal Court and a tribunal investigating genocide in Rwanda.

But it was Ms. Pillay’s work last year on a U.N. commission on Israel that made the Nobel committee’s announcement on Friday an intensely political decision, as it put the prize in the middle of one of the world’s most divisive issues.

That commission said that Israel was committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, a finding that Israel rejected.

Announcing the award, the Nobel committee did not explicitly mention Gaza, instead citing Ms. Pillay’s long career in human rights and a global shift toward “power politics” that had undermined respect for law and justice. The committee chair, Jorgen Watne Frydnes, called the award “a message to those who are attacking” international law.

Ms. Pillay, 85, is “one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said, calling her “instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted.”

The office of Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, quickly denounced the committee in a statement, calling its members misguided and saying it had “lost its moral compass.” It also condemned Ms. Pillay’s work, accusing her of being prejudiced against Jews.

The Israeli foreign ministry went further, calling the Nobel decision a “grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.”

After learning she had won the award, Ms. Pillay, speaking at a conference of human rights lawyers in Nuremberg, Germany, said she had tried to hew only to the law and facts in her career, not politics.

“Why would you need courage to speak the truth?” she said. “You interpret the law, you look at all the facts. So it’s an impartial, you know, impartial decision-making.”

Her work on Israel and Gaza, though, was “an important part of the reasoning why she received the prize,” Mr. Frydnes, the Nobel committee chair, told reporters.

President Trump, who has been a staunch supporter of Israel and has openly angled to win the Nobel Peace Prize himself, did not immediately address Friday’s award. He did, however, share a post on his social media platform that called Ms. Pillay “an unabashed hater of America and Israel” and said that it was Mr. Trump who deserved the prize.

After receiving the news at the conference in Nuremberg, Ms. Pillay was applauded by more than a hundred fellow attendees, a video posted by the Amnesty International head, Agnès Callamard, showed.

“If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump,” Ms. Pillay joked, apparently referring to last year’s winner, María Corina Machado, the Venezuelan opposition leader who presented her medal to the U.S. president in January.

At a brief news conference, Ms. Pillay mused that “perhaps it was meant to be” that she had received the news in Nuremberg, a city whose famous postwar trials of Nazi leaders were foundational to creating the modern international justice system.

“We are living through an era when international law and human rights are under significant political attack,” she said. Such efforts, she said, were “particularly visible with the attacks on the International Criminal Court,” which the Trump administration has vowed to dismantle “brick by brick.”

Born to a family of Indian Tamil origin, the daughter of a homemaker and a bus driver, Ms. Pillay was one of seven children who grew up in poverty in the city of Durban, on South Africa’s east coast. She came of age in a segregated city, attending a school for Indian South Africans.

As a teenager, Ms. Pillay said, she experienced apartheid’s daily injustices and witnessed the violent crackdown by police forces and vigilantes on Black South African protesters and their supporters.

“The government was oppressive, the laws were oppressive and the courts cooperated with these laws,” she said in a video published by the I.C.C. in 2017. “We had no remedies, and as a 15-year-old, I wished that we could appeal to a higher system of law, a higher institution, so that we, the victims, can get justice.”

Ms. Pillay pursued a law degree and later defended imprisoned anti-apartheid activists, including Nelson Mandela, many of whom faced terrorism charges and placed under surveillance. After the end of apartheid, Ms. Pillay became a judge on the High Court in South Africa, where she championed women’s rights and equality.

Soon, Ms. Pillay was drawn into international human rights crises. In 1995, Mr. Mandela — then South Africa’s president — appointed her as a judge at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda.

Ms. Pillay is the fifth South African to be awarded the peace prize, after Mr. Mandela, the activist Albert Luthuli, former President F.W. de Klerk and Desmond Tutu, the cleric who helped bring down apartheid.

One of Ms. Pillay’s contributions to international law was her pioneering work on the gravity of sexual violence during the Rwanda conflict. In a trial at the tribunal, she pushed from the bench to define rape of women and children as a weapon of war.

In 1998, when the tribunal found a former Rwandan mayor guilty of genocide, it was the first time that rape had been defined as part of genocide. Sexual violence has since been integrated in international law as a potential war crime, a crime against humanity or an act of genocide.

Two decades later, in 2019, Ms. Pillay served as an ad hoc judge on the International Court of Justice in a case in which Myanmar was accused of genocide against the Rohingya Muslim minority.

Even as her work expanded beyond South Africa, she remained a prominent voice for human rights in the country, speaking out against anti-immigrant violence that flared in Durban in 2015 and chiding the South African government for having considered leaving the I.C.C. in 2016.

This year’s selection is the latest in a line of decisions by the Norwegian Nobel Committee that have carried political weight.

The year before awarding the prize to Ms. Machado, the Venezuelan opposition leader, the committee honored Nihon Hidankyo, a Japanese organization representing atomic bomb survivors, many of whom have campaigned for nuclear disarmament. In 2023, the prize went to Narges Mohammadi, Iran’s most prominent human rights activist.

item.title: Large Earthquake in Panama Sets Off Tsunami Alert
item.description:
An earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 7.7 hit the Central American nation of Panama on Friday, shaking buildings in Panama City and prompting evacuations, according to the U.S. Geological Survey and videos posted on social media. Tsunami alerts affecting the region followed.

The quake hit about 1:56 p.m. Eastern time, according to the U.S.G.S. It was centered about nine miles southwest of Pitaloza Arriba, a town in the country’s southern Azuero Peninsula. It was followed by at least three strong aftershocks in the following hour.

In Panama City, the capital, northeast of the earthquake’s epicenter, buildings shook and people evacuated into the streets, according to video footage posted on social media. About 2 million people live in the capital region.

The quake prompted the U.S. Pacific Tsunami Warning Center to issue alerts along the Pacific Coast of several Central American countries. Hazardous waves that could reach up to 10 feet above tide levels are possible in Panama. The center said waves up to a foot above normal were possible in countries with Pacific Ocean coastlines from Ecuador to New Zealand, the center said.

No immediate threats were reported for the United States.

Aurelio Martínez, a spokesman for the Panamanian national police, said in a brief phone interview that there damage had been reported in the interior of the country, including in the Veraguas Province in Central Panama. But he said that it was too soon to tell how much structural damage the country had sustained, and if there were any injuries or deaths.

The U.S. Embassy in Panama said there were no initial reports of injuries among its staff or at the embassy.

This is a developing story and will be updated.

Jack Nicas and John Keefe contributed reporting.

item.title: Attacker in FlyDubai Flight Meant to Crash Into Israeli Airport, Emiratis Say
item.description:
Emirati investigators said on Friday that the co-pilot who attacked the captain of a FlyDubai flight last week had developed extremist Islamist views over several years and had intended to carry out a Sept. 11-inspired suicide crash into Israel’s biggest airport.

The details, disclosed by the Emirati attorney general, offered the most comprehensive official account so far of the co-pilot’s motives and preparation. The report also deepened questions about how signs of his radicalization were missed before he was allowed to fly such a sensitive route.

More than 170 passengers, mostly Israelis, were on FlyDubai Flight 1073 last week when the co-pilot began attacking the pilot with the plane’s crash ax and then tried to crash the airliner. The pilot, Capt. Smit Machchhar, managed to unlock the cockpit door, and passengers were able to subdue the assailant, narrowly averting a catastrophe.

Backup pilots were on board and ultimately stabilized the plane, bringing it to an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

The Emirati attorney general, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, said the co-pilot, a 29-year-old Omani national, had planned to crash the plane into the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv “with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life.”

The Emirati statement did not identify the co-pilot, but people familiar with the investigation have said that his name is Hamam al-Hammami, and that his embrace of radical Islamist views prompted the Omani authorities to scrutinize him earlier.

The Emirati investigation found that the co-pilot had begun a “drift towards extremism and terrorism” almost a decade ago, while he was a student in Melbourne, Australia. The Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology said in a statement that the co-pilot was enrolled at the university between 2015 and 2017 but did not complete his engineering degree.

While in Australia, Mr. al-Hammami developed a fascination with extremist literature and online content “glorifying terrorist organizations and suicide operations” the Emirati statement said. He also “received support” from groups related to the Muslim Brotherhood, an international Islamist movement, according to the statement, without elaborating further.

Taking inspiration from the attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, and takfir ideology — a view that effectively allows one Muslim to declare another an apostate — the co-pilot became increasingly interested in a similar attack, the Emirati statement said.

He confessed to the authorities that following through on that vision was “linked to his decision to pursue a career in aviation,” according to investigators. Before coming to FlyDubai in January 2026, he was employed by Oman Air for four years and spent a brief stint at Royal Maroc Air, a Moroccan airline, the investigation found.

The co-pilot told the authorities that he acted alone, investigators said, though they added that were still looking into that question. To prepare for the operation, he had used two previous flights to Tel Aviv to familiarize himself with the route, consumed more “material promoting terrorism” and trained in boxing, the Emirati statement said.

But the disclosure left open questions about how Mr. al-Hammami was cleared to fly such a sensitive route. It is unclear whether Omani investigators had shared their concerns with security officials in Israel, the United Arab Emirates — where the flight originated — or with the airline.

Mr. Al Shamsi said the co-pilot “had met the professional and security requirements for employment” at FlyDubai, including completing required checks and providing a certificate of “good conduct.” He added that none of the steps revealed “any indications of his extremist views or his intention to carry out a terrorist plot.”

The plane’s passengers were mostly Israelis, some of whom said the crisis evoked the feelings of dread they had last felt on Oct. 7, 2023, during the Hamas-led attack on Israel, in which about 1,200 people were killed.

After the failed attack on the plane, two posts appeared on a LinkedIn profile bearing Mr. al-Hammami’s name. One depicted a photo of Ayman al-Zawahri, who led Al Qaeda after Osama bin Laden’s death and was killed by the United States in 2022. It was not clear who made the posts or whether they had been scheduled in advance to be published.

Victoria Kim contributed reporting.

item.title: India’s Young Put Their Bodies on the Line to Be Heard
item.description:
After the police repeatedly detained her as she climbed over barricades blocking the protest site in India’s capital, Neha Bora took to Instagram last weekend.

The 29-year-old activist, who has become a prominent face of the season of discontent gripping India, shared the day’s accumulation of bruises with her more than one million followers, leaning into the style of a fitness influencer.

“This is my bicep, this is my tricep,” she said, rolling up her sleeves and pointing to each mark. “And see here — I had a shoulder day, too.”

Then, looking straight into the camera, she unleashed her fury at the Delhi police. Their intimidation would not stop the youth, she said.

“We will march again tomorrow,” she said. “To tell you that you can’t snatch our freedom, our right to protest.”

Protests, marches and strikes of all kinds were once common in the capital. But the space for dissent in India has shrunk over the last decade under Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and recently his government has refused to allow protests even in the one “designated area” called Jantar Mantar that they had been reduced to in New Delhi. Instead, over the past week columns of security forces have been moving in to pick up anyone daring to gather in the area.

But for months, India’s young have been putting their bodies on the line to be heard. The battle-lines are drawn, with youth groups calling for their biggest march yet on Saturday.

During the summer, they demanded the resignation of the education minister over repeated scandals in college entrance exams. Some protesters, including Ms. Bora, went on extended hunger strikes. The protests only grew, and the police unleashed water cannons, tear gas, and even pellet guns, causing widespread outrage. The government made a rare concession and the minister quit.

The protesters have taken to the streets again. This time they are voicing anger over the culling of more than 130 million names from India’s voter roll, which they argue was a political move to favor Mr. Modi’s party, which the ruling party denies. They are demanding the resignation of the country’s election commission chief.

Their sustained pressure on the streets, and creative use of social media, has opened a crack in the powerful hold that Mr. Modi established during his dozen years in office — something the traditional political opposition struggled to do.

Ms. Bora, a doctoral student in theater studies who is the president of the leftist All India Students’ Association, said the outpouring of anger was a sign that any strongman can consolidate power “only to a certain extent.”

“I’m not saying that people are completely at ease and they’re comfortable and the democracy is flourishing,” she said. “But people are not afraid of the police anymore.”

On the streets of Delhi, protesters have engaged in a game of cat and mouse, finding inventive ways to evade attempts by the police to block them.

Last Sunday, Ms. Bora climbed the first layer of barricades, trying to reach the designated protest site.

As police officers tried to hold the protesters back, she was fuming. After much push and pull, she managed to jump to the other side, and soon the police line was broken.

Protesters dragged the barricades apart, only to face another layer of barricades and more columns of police. The police dragged protesters one by one onto buses, driving them away into detention.

Ms. Bora was detained six times over two days; the last time, she said, the police drove her tens of miles and dropped her off in an industrial area.

“By the time you’re released and you come back to central Delhi or wherever the protest is taking place, you are so tired and night has set in, so you can’t again start the protest,” she said. “It’s part of their playbook.”

One group of volunteers developed an app to track the buses protesters are packed into. By tracing their route, the app connects them with volunteer drivers who can rush them back, as well as legal and medical help.

“Most of the people are students, women, people protesting for the first time, and they don’t know what to do,” said Rajiv Choudhary, 25, who helped develop the app. “We created a system to say, ‘No worries, we are behind you, we are sending some help.’”

In detention, the protesters continued to poke the authorities, training their cameras on the messy state of affairs.

“Guys, we have been detained in this police station,” says one young protester in an Instagram video. “But look at this — how dirty the water, this area, is.”

At the barricades near the protest site, as the young people were picked up, some older people who had come in solidarity stepped up.

Nisha Sidhu, 62, gave the police an earful. They leaned on the barricades, staring at her.

“In his speeches, the prime minister says ‘educate your daughters,’” she said. “But when they come here to ask for their rights, you try to silence them? It doesn’t look like we live in a free country.”

item.title: Labour Holds Off Green Party in Election for Starmer’s Former London Seat
item.description:
The Labour Party in Britain held onto the parliamentary seat vacated by former Prime Minister Keir Starmer, winning a special election in central London that was seen as an early test for Andy Burnham, Mr. Starmer’s successor.

Sagal Abdi-Wali, who is currently the Labour Party leader of the local Camden Council, defeated the Green Party hopeful and other candidates to retain the Holborn and St. Pancras seat for her party.

She won with 45 percent of the vote, according to results announced in the early hours of Friday morning.

Ms. Abdi-Wali, who was born in Somalia and came to Britain as a child refugee in the 1990s, campaigned for many of the same policies that Mr. Burnham laid out in a speech at the Labour conference last month.

“Opportunities for young people, ending rough sleeping on our streets, making things like water bills more affordable and a safe, secure home,” she wrote in a recent online article. “These are my big priorities for Camden. But most of all — I want to give you hope again.”

The victory, while expected, is a boost to Mr. Burnham, who took over as the country’s leader after helping to engineer Mr. Starmer’s ouster over the summer. Surveys suggest that Mr. Burnham is popular with the public, and under his leadership, the party is once more leading in national polls. But he faces the same fundamental challenges that his predecessor did: a sluggish economy, rising prices and government bond yields because of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, and not enough money to pay for all the competing priorities.

Ms. Abdi-Wali defeated, among others, Zack Polanski, the leader of Britain’s Green Party, who was seeking his own seat in Parliament. Mr. Polanski ended up with 33 percent of the vote.

Mr. Polanski’s party has been having more success in British politics recently, and he had hoped that a victory in the central London district would add to the sense of momentum for the movement he leads.

But his political success has been marred by several controversies in recent months. Over the weekend, a small group of Green Party activists voted at the party’s annual conference to declare that Zionism is racism, a move that infuriated many supporters of Israel.

The measure passed with just over 1,000 votes out of the 1,800 cast at the conference. The party has more than 230,000 members. Mr. Polanski did not vote for the measure, but he has refused to criticize it. Asked later by the BBC about the motion, he said: “If your Zionism is the displacement of the Palestinian people, then that is clearly racist, and I say that as a Jewish leader of a British political party.”

item.title: France’s Long, Fervent History of Protest
item.description:
Do you hear the people sing?

On Thursday, thousands of protesters, many of them high schoolers, broke out into the national anthem at Place de la Bastille, where in 1789 a mob stormed a royal prison, touching off the French Revolution.

Protests are so embedded in French political life that “the streets” are considered a fourth branch of government, a last resort when the legislative, executive and judicial are unresponsive, according to David A. Bell, a history professor at Princeton University.

Modern France sprang out of a bloody revolt in 1789, whose symbolism has been invoked in movements ever since, as it was on Thursday. From street revolts throughout the 19th century — including a short-lived one in 1832 that inspired “Les Misérables” — to the Yellow Vest protests that began in 2018, that tradition has thrived.

France also possesses a distinct political culture, said Julian Bourg, a history professor at Boston College. “In contrast to the Anglo-American tradition, which sees the state as some foreign, invasive body threatening individual freedom, in France, there’s a long tradition that the state embodies the people,” he said, and that the state is thus “directly accountable to the people.”

Most importantly, Mr. Bell said, protests are common because of a sense that they work. Demonstrations in the 1930s led to worker protections that are still jealously guarded. And French leaders have offered some concessions in recent protests — though some advocates have dismissed those as a “smoke screen.”

Certain aspects set these protests apart. For the first time in decades, Mr. Bourg said, high school students were the first to act. And historians also note the role of social media in allowing movements to spread like wildfire, as opposed to uprisings from past generations that took longer to ripple out from Paris.

Nevertheless, the demonstrations of recent weeks contain undeniable and instructive echoes of the past. Here are some protests in modern French history that put today’s student movement in context.

Twenty-first century demonstrations cannot be understood outside of those that swept across France in 1968, which transformed the country.

“We’re the heirs of May ’68,” proclaimed a banner outside a school last week. That year, protests led by university students spurred millions of workers to strike and nearly toppled the government, inspiring similar student movements abroad.

Mr. Bourg cautioned that, so far, the demonstrations in recent weeks have been more tightly focused and not as ideologically potent as those that roiled France nearly 60 years ago, fueled at first by radical, anti-establishment politics.

“That said, each major French protest movement does raise the possibility that the demands of a specific cohort may lead to more generalized protest and a broader political crisis,” he said. “That is the echo of 1968.”

Teachers, parents, university students and union leaders have rallied their support behind student demonstrators demanding better conditions and more teachers in high schools.

France faced a three-week convulsion across hundreds of suburbs and towns in 2005 after two teenagers, Zyed Benna and Bouna Traoré, were electrocuted while hiding from police in an electrical substation.

Fiery clashes between protesters and the police arose amid long-simmering tensions over youth unemployment and accusations of police brutality, especially against low-income people and people of color in high-rise banlieues, or suburbs, of Paris and other cities.

Many of those tensions remain unresolved. The police killing of a teenage boy in 2023 set off mass protests, after which thousands of minors were arrested.

Though current protests have focused on demands for education reform, much of the anger stems from an enduring sense among young people that political leaders are not sufficiently invested in their futures.

In 2018, the “Yellow Vest” protests — spurred by an increase in the gasoline tax and named for the roadside safety vests worn by the demonstrators — emerged as a spontaneous outcry over declining living standards.

The demonstrations flared late in 2018 and continued with periodic surges into 2020. Protesters broke into government buildings, the police fired rubber bullets and tear gas, and several people died in traffic incidents related to the demonstrations.

Mr. Bourg said there was not a clear partisan valence for the yellow vests, though the decentralized populist movement directed its anger against the economic policies of President Emmanuel Macron, whose final term will end early next year. And like current protests, Mr. Bell said, the yellow vest movement began with a focus on a singular issue. But it evolved to express frustrations over broader austerity measures.

Mr. Macron also sparked outrage in 2023 when he proposed raising the legal retirement age to 64 from 62.

The outcry that followed drove more than a million people into the streets in some cases. Workers in disparate industries and across the political spectrum demonstrated against the proposed changes, which the government insisted were necessary steps to help address a budget crisis.

Mr. Macron used a rare procedure to push the new retirement age into law without a vote of the Parliament, reinforcing his image as an imperious leader.

Last year, after prolonged political turbulence, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu stunned the country by offering to pause the change until after the next presidential election, in 2027.

item.title: A Rural Village Voted to Leave the U.K., Stirring Britain’s Migration Debate
item.description:
“What a week we’ve had,” a triumphant Tim McNally told dozens of his neighbors in Piddington’s village hall.

“I said to you guys, we are going to turn Piddington, this small village, into the largest village on this earth,” Mr. McNally, the chair of the parish council, said on a Tuesday night in late September. “That we are going to put it on the map.”

And they had.

The village of just over 350 people voted on Sept. 15 to become independent of the United Kingdom, in protest against a government plan to house 1,250 male asylum seekers in a nearby former military site.

Piddington has not, in fact, broken away from the United Kingdom, as the referendum had no legal basis. But it catapulted the rural village in Oxfordshire to the top of news sites and social media feeds, a publicity coup that Mr. McNally likened to a “blueprint” for other places facing the possible arrival of asylum seekers.

Piddington swiftly became an example of how a small place could challenge a national government over concerns that inhabitants felt were being ignored. In this case, how could a small village with no shops or pubs cope with more than a thousand unemployed men suddenly on its outskirts?

The campaign, which at times amplified far-right talking points about immigrants, also illustrated how divisive migration has become around Europe. In Britain, while asylum applications are down since a peak late last year, they remain consistently higher than the pre-2021 average.

The highly visible arrival of migrants crossing the English Channel, almost all of whom apply for asylum, has become a flashpoint, though these small boat arrivals have also declined since their highest level in 2022.

The Piddington vote underlined a dilemma confronting many European governments: Where should asylum seekers be housed as their applications are processed and anti-immigrant sentiment becomes more forceful and widespread?

Among the locals opposing the plan was Melise Witkin, 59, who said the proximity of the site to a village green, the Jubilee Reserve, was worrying.

“No one in their right mind is going to want to walk around the Jubilee worried that they might come down the road and there might be 20 of them,” Ms. Witkin, 59, said of asylum seekers. “They might be the loveliest, loveliest guys, but what if they’re not?”

That perceived threat to women and children from the arrival of many unemployed men was a focus of the village vote. In Britain, asylum seekers have been barred from working since the early 2000s, and the government has a legal obligation to provide accommodation while claims are processed.

The former military site, on the village outskirts, would house 18- to 65-year-old men, according to the proposals. They would be allowed to come and go during the day.

Rachel Marsh, 54, also opposes the plan, believing the location unsuitable and the militarized setup inhumane. But she was one of 26 residents who voted against independence, after becoming uncomfortable with the campaign’s tone.

“They have fallen for the fear rhetoric — hook, line, and sinker,” she said of some neighbors. She felt sad, she said, that misinformation about immigrants being disproportionately violent or criminal was being used “to whip people into this radicalized frenzy.” (While data is limited, researchers say there is little evidence that immigration has an impact on overall crime rates.)

The independence campaign’s Facebook account, which Mr. McNally and others run, shared an A.I.-generated animation that depicts an idyllic-looking village populated by white people, who appear terrified and dismayed as shirtless Black men march and leer at young girls, while men in turbans scare children out of a playground.

The campaign, and Mr. McNally specifically, tagged and thanked right-wing activists and figures such as Elon Musk, who has regularly used social media to attempt to influence British politics. In an interview, Mr. McNally said Mr. Musk’s resharing of a campaign post was a positive turning point.

“I thought, right, we’re definitely onto something here,” he said, adding that it helped push a “narrative” about the risks to the community. When asked about accusations that xenophobic and racist imagery was used in campaign videos, he said he did not create the clips. “I don’t see it as racism at all,” he said, adding, “It’s telling the story of Piddington and as far as I am concerned, that is an accurate representation.”

In Britain more broadly, anger over immigration has grown in recent years and protests against asylum seekers have become disruptive and at times violent.

In September, hundreds of anti-migrant demonstrators wearing balaclavas gathered in Portsmouth, in southern England, blocking port access for several hours. This week, another group clashed with the police in Gosport, a coastal town where migrants were brought ashore on a rescue boat.

The backlash over using military sites follows an earlier outcry over the use of hotels for asylum accommodation, by the previous Conservative government, to comply with social distancing rules. After the pandemic, the number of people crossing the English Channel in small boats to claim asylum rose rapidly, while the processing of claims slowed, leading to a large backlog that the Labour government has only partly cut.

Shabana Mahmood, Labour’s home secretary who is responsible for immigration policies, has embraced a hard-line approach in an effort to show the government has heard voters’ concerns. Using former military sites instead of hotels — to create the perception of a less generous and more controlled approach — is part of that.

But efforts to convert military sites can be costly, high-profile and polarizing, said Sunder Katwala, director of British Future, a research organization in London. They also give agitators a place to go, and create a situation where locals’ concerns appear to be ignored, he said.

“That’s the one thing we should be trying to do: separate out real concerns from agitation and stirring up trouble,” he said. “What we don’t want, I think, is to cross the wires, where the reasonable parish council meeting attendee is now in receipt of extreme conspiracy narratives from the very far right.”

There is little doubt that Piddington residents genuinely oppose the site. A separate initiative, Wrong Plan, Wrong Site, is mounting evidence-based legal challenges to the proposal. But it has taken a back seat to the independence campaign’s more provocative arguments.

“None of that balance was brought into the equation,” Ms. Marsh said. She added, however, that the Labour government’s failure to listen to concerns had created space for vitriolic voices, saying: “Labour’s refusal to engage with the people on this has handed it to the far right.”

She and her husband have lived in Piddington for two decades and raised their children here. She is originally from New Zealand, and her husband’s parents were from the Windrush generation of Caribbean people who migrated legally to Britain after World War II.

After Ms. Marsh was interviewed on the BBC on the day of the referendum, she and her family received an onslaught of online abuse. An anti-immigrant campaigner arrived at her home, filmed her and published the footage, showing her address. The clip was shared by far-right agitators, and she met with the police to discuss her safety.

Still, Ms. Marsh said it remained important to offer an alternative perspective. “I do think there is an agenda here to keep us divided,” she said.

Piddington has been here before. In 2001, a plan to develop asylum accommodation outside the village also drew intense opposition. It was scrapped when the government determined it wasn’t economically viable.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last week that the military site was being considered because voters had wanted people out of hotels.

“But I’ve heard what people are saying in Piddington and the other places affected,” he said. “I don’t ignore their concerns.”

In a statement, the Home Office said it plans to close asylum hotels and move people to alternative accommodation, including former military sites “designed to be self-contained, with 24/7 security and CCTV, to reduce the impact on local communities.”

item.title: Paintings Stolen From Renoir Museum Are Recovered, Authorities Say
item.description:
Two Renoir paintings that were stolen from a museum in southern France last month have been recovered, and six suspects have been arrested in the case, the city where the theft took place said in a statement on Friday.

The artworks — a portrait of the French actress Colonna Romano, painted around 1910, and “Young Woman at the Well,” an oil painting from around 1886 — were stolen from a museum that is a former home of the Impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir in the town of Cagnes-Sur-Mer.

The robbery, which the authorities said at the time was carried out by two people, was the latest in a series of brazen thefts from cultural and religious sites in France, including a heist in which royal jewels worth over $100 million were taken from the Louvre about a year ago.

The thieves at the Renoir museum initially took four paintings, but left two behind in the garden as they scrambled to evade the police, who arrived at the scene five minutes after the security alarm went off.

The mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer, Bryan Masson, said in the city’s statement, that the recovered paintings were “part of our city’s history, our cultural heritage and the legacy Auguste Renoir left to Cagnes-sur-Mer.”

“Their recovery is a tremendous relief for the people of Cagnes-sur-Mer and for everyone who cares deeply about our museum,” he added.

Catherine Pégard, the national culture minister, said on social media that the recovery was a “huge relief.”

“These paintings are part of our collective memory,” she said. “They will now be able to return to Renoir’s final resting place, a site steeped in history and dear to both residents and visitors from around the world.”

item.title: In a Dead Hero’s Ashes, El Salvador’s Ruler Finds a New Spark
item.description:
The sun was just about to set in El Salvador one September day when President Nayib Bukele debuted his new passion project. Even by the exacting standards of Latin American political showmanship, it was jaw-dropping.

Clad like a Napoleonic general in a uniform adorned with gold trim, Mr. Bukele strode past bayonet-wielding soldiers, unsheathed a sword and laid it atop newly disinterred human remains.

In state-produced videos, Mr. Bukele told millions of social media followers that an urn with what is left of Francisco Morazán, a 19th-century Central American ruler, had just been placed into a crypt where it would be safeguarded “forever.”

“Francisco Morazán was born Honduran,” said Mr. Bukele. “But he lived, fought, and died as a Central American.”

The spectacle trained a new spotlight on Mr. Bukele, who has gutted democratic guardrails, made mass arrests and slashed crime rates, all while enjoying towering popular support. The Bukele-dominated Congress scrapped term limits, enabling him to remain in power indefinitely.

While doing so, Mr. Bukele has emerged as a top ally of President Trump in Latin America, transforming the small country into a hub for imprisoning deportees from the United States while trolling elected Democrats opposing the Trump administration.

Mr. Bukele has amassed so much power that the display of pomp created a stir across Central America: Why was he digging up a long-dead figure who was already resting in El Salvador’s most distinguished cemetery?

Manuel Zometa, an El Salvador-based constitutional law specialist and a rare vocal critic in a system hostile to dissent, called Mr. Bukele’s new mausoleum a bid to assert greater dominance over the country’s political landscape.

“His popularity is starting to soften,” Mr. Zometa said, citing polls showing Mr. Bukele’s sky-high approval ratings falling slightly as economic concerns over rising inflation and unemployment intensify. “Facing the diminishing returns of his war on crime, he reverted to the playbook tactic of exhuming a national hero.”

Latin America boasts a rich tradition of political exhumations, with leaders using such rituals to advance their own ambitions regardless of how they might disturb the long-entombed’s search for tranquillity in the hereafter.

While Mr. Bukele rules from the right, he is following examples set this century prominently on the left. (Representatives for Mr. Bukele did not respond to a request for comment.)

Hugo Chávez, the late ruler of Venezuela, disinterred the liberation hero Simón Bolívar, then deposited the remains in a colossal new mausoleum. Similarly, Rafael Correa, a former president of Ecuador, transferred the ashes of Eloy Alfaro, a leader beheaded by a mob, to a new mausoleum.

Mr. Bukele’s latest twist on this custom already seems to be paying political dividends. Guides say thousands of visitors a day are streaming into the new mausoleum, located in a once rundown hotel in the historic core of San Salvador, the capital.

Throngs of street vendors have been removed from the high-security enclave. Surrounding streets have the look of being scrubbed clean. A futuristic new $54 million national library given as a gift by China stands directly across from the mausoleum.

Once inside the new climate-controlled crypt, guides expound on Morazán’s historical importance. Soldiers in vintage dress uniforms try to remain motionless as they stand guard before the remains.

Grecia Montserrat, 22, came with her mother to see what the hubbub was about. She had only a vague idea of who Morazán was, she said, because, in her view, leftist authorities had previously “only taught us to admire guerrillas.”

Ms. Montserrat, an undergraduate studying graphic design, said she was impressed by the mausoleum’s freshly painted facade and the fact that the building is open most days, admission free, until midnight.

“The whole thing makes me proud to be Salvadoran,” she said.

Still, some historians have found Mr. Bukele’s decision to exalt the Honduran-born Morazán perplexing since El Salvador has traditionally venerated another 19th-century ruler, the Salvadoran-born Gerardo Barrios, as a founding father.

Morazán was seen more as a regional leader because of his role as the force behind the Federal Republic of Central America, an attempt in the 1820s to merge former provinces of the Spanish Empire into a single, sovereign state.

That project fell apart, and a firing squad of insurgent forces executed Morazán in 1842 in Costa Rica. He stipulated in his will that he wanted to be buried in El Salvador.

But Morazán is also considered the founding father of neighboring Honduras, where that country’s top military academy, major plazas, boulevards, public schools and a weeklong commemoration bear his name.

Chafing at the new crypt, Honduran commentators called for Morazán’s remains to be repatriated and argued that Mr. Bukele was theatrically trying to lift his regional profile in a ploy to emerge as Central America’s unrivaled leader.

“He’s styling himself as a modern-day Morazán,” the Honduran historian Jorge Amaya said in televised comments, contending that Mr. Bukele had even begun dressing in a style channeling Morazán’s martial flair, a departure from the backward baseball cap and rolled-up sleeves of his earlier look.

Other doubts about the mausoleum have emerged. After Morazán’s execution, he was cremated and his ashes spent years shuffling between different churches in El Salvador before they were finally interred in 1858.

But during a siege of San Salvador in 1863, forces loyal to an invading Guatemalan strongman were said to have desecrated, and possibly destroyed, the monument holding the ashes.

“It’s very difficult to determine at this point, some 180 years after the fact, whether these remains are truly his,” said Alfredo Ramírez, a historian at the University of El Salvador.

For those streaming into the mausoleum, such details seemed like background noise.

Omar Sosa, 57, who said he fled El Salvador for the United States decades ago and now returns occasionally to visit, said he was overcome with emotion when he approached the crypt.

The solemn tribute to Morazán showed that the strife-torn nation he knew as a youth had been transformed, said Mr. Sosa, who owns two convenience stores in Austin, Texas.

“We were always the bad apple,” he said. “But now this country is an example for the world.”
